_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a3.1: I compared him to you: in part, but not to all your offerings. However, [that he may bring] a burnt offering is reasonable, since it is fit [for him], as it is entirely burnt.
rashi:a4.1: Circumcision, immersion and the sprinkling of blood: it explains below.
rashi:a6.1: “And [the priest] shall sacrifice it”: stated about the voluntary bird burnt offering in [the book of] Leviticus.
rashi:a6.2: “And he shall sacrifice” [vehikriv]: implies a complete offering.
rashi:a8.1: All the people who left: at the time of their departure they were circumcised.
rashi:a8.2: In your blood: the blood of the Paschal offering and the blood of circumcision.
rashi:a9.1: The sprinkling [hartza’at] of blood: the sprinkling of blood on the altar.
rashi:a10.1: “And if a stranger sojourn with you” … “throughout your generations”: even though there is no Temple.
rashi:a11.1: He must set aside a quarter dinar for his nest: so that when the Temple is built he will bring a nest, since we said above that he requires an offering. And it is impossible to set aside [money for] an offering with less than a quarter, for a nest is not available for less than a quarter, as we say in the mishna [above, 8a]: “And nests stood at a quarter-dinar each”; but less is not possible.
rashi:a11.2: Due to a mishap: lest he derive benefit from it.
rashi:a12.1: Ger toshav: one who accepted upon himself not to worship idols, such as Naaman.
rashi:a12.2: Performs labor on Shabbat for himself: in a matter that would otherwise be lost, like a Jew on the intermediate days of a Festival.
rashi:a13.1: Like a Jew on a Festival: [labor for] food.
rashi:a14.1: Mishna. The oath of testimony: [he brings] a sliding-scale offering.
rashi:a14.2: The oath on a deposit: [he brings] a guilt offering.
rashi:a17.1: Gemara. Since it could have written “for his sin” and stopped, and it writes “for his sin that he has sinned,” [this comes] to include many sins.
rashi:a17.2: “And he shall be forgiven for his sin that he has sinned”: this is why it writes “sin” twice more, besides the first two times: to make intentional like unwitting. [Rashi’s wording here is “to make intentional like unwitting”; the daf at this line reads “to make unwitting like intentional.”]
rashi:a19.1: “And the Lord spoke suddenly”: the three of them went out by the divine word against their will.
rashi:a20.1: “But the thoughtless pass on, and are punished”: this is intentional, for there is no punishment except for intentional sin.
rashi:a22.1: I would have said: although “suddenly” elsewhere implies circumstances beyond one’s control, unwitting and intentional, the “suddenly” of the nazirite is certainly unwitting, since he brings an offering for it, just as in the entire Torah, where most offerings come for unwitting sins. That is why “unexpectedly,” which is unwitting, is written: to reveal about “suddenly” [that it means beyond his control and intentional].
rashi:a24.1: In all of them: in all who bring a sliding-scale offering in that passage, such as one who renders the Temple impure and the oath of utterance, which are written together with the oath of testimony.
rashi:a28.1: To make intentional like unwitting; but the verse itself is written about intentional sin: for it is written: “There shall be an inspection [bikoret]” (Leviticus 19:20), which is lashes, and there are lashes only for intentional sin; and about that it says: “And he shall bring his guilt offering.” Why, then, do I need “and he shall be forgiven for his sin” to include intentional sin?
rashi:a28.2: Rather, say: to make unwitting like intentional: for you might have said that he brings [an offering] only for intentional sin and not for unwitting sin. It teaches us: “And he shall be forgiven for his sin that he has sinned.” That is why “sin” is written four times: two to derive one offering for many transgressions, and two to make unwitting like intentional.
rashi:a29.1: In one lapse of awareness: that is, before he was flogged and brought an offering for this one, he went back and had relations with that one.
rashi:a31.1: Did you not say about forbidden relations: in the first chapter (above, 2b): “And unto a woman,” to divide for each and every woman, and so on.
tosafot:a1.1: One might have thought that I include even a meal offering: meaning the meal offering of libations, which goes entirely to the fires [of the altar].
tosafot:a3.1: The verse states: “As you are, so shall the stranger be”: it could have said, as above [8b]: Now that a bird was included, [would an animal not all the more so be included]?
tosafot:a8.1: As it is written: “For all the people were circumcised”: meaning that they circumcised themselves at their exodus from Egypt. And although those who had been circumcised [following the practice] from the days of Abraham were not circumcised at the exodus from Egypt, nevertheless, originally, when they circumcised themselves, they circumcised in order to enter the covenant of the Omnipresent and to be separated from the other nations; and also now they immersed.
tosafot:a9.1: “And he sent the young men of the children of Israel, and they offered burnt offerings”: and although they disagree there, in the chapter Parat Ḥatat (Zevaḥim 115b), some saying it was the burnt offering of appearance and some saying it was the daily burnt offering, one can say that they offered many burnt offerings.
tosafot:a9.2: “And sprinkled it on the people”: they slaughtered many burnt offerings and many peace offerings, whose blood sufficed to be sprinkled on each and every one of Israel.
tosafot:a9.3: And there is no sprinkling without immersion: [this comes] to include a convert who comes to convert in the present time: he requires immersion.
tosafot:a11.1: He must set aside a quarter, etc.: this is not like a zava and a woman after childbirth, who do not set aside [money], because their offering serves to make them fit for sacrificial food; but a convert brings an offering to permit him to enter the congregation.
tosafot:a11.2: The halakha is in accordance with Rabbi Shimon: who says that a ger and a resident slave and maidservant perform labor for themselves as a Jew does on a weekday; and specifically for themselves, and not for others.
tosafot:a13.1: Like a Jew on a Festival: for about him [the ger] only “refreshment” in general [yinafesh, Exodus 23:12] is written, and not “cessation” [shevita].
tosafot:a13.2: [This refers to the line above:] A ger toshav performs labor for himself: from here there is a difficulty for Rashi’s explanation in the chapter HaḤoletz (Yevamot 48b), where it says: “And the son of your maidservant and the stranger may be refreshed” (Exodus 23:12), this is a ger toshav; and Rashi explained in his commentary: one who accepted upon himself not to worship idols, and who desecrates Shabbat like a gentile. And here it says that a ger toshav performs labor. Therefore one can say that that [verse] speaks of not performing labor on behalf of his master, but for himself it is permitted. (Ruling:) From here the Ri ruled that it is permitted to let a gentile perform his own labor on Shabbat in a Jew’s house, for himself.
tosafot:a22.1: I would have said: when he brings an offering, it is for unwitting sin, etc.: this is puzzling: if so, let the verse write [a term meaning] unwitting.
gershom:a1.1: (Up to here belongs to 8b.) Rabbi says: “As you,” as your ancestors: just as your ancestors entered the covenant only through circumcision, immersion and the sprinkling of blood. Rabbi does not hold like Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov, that he brings an offering in order to eat sacrificial food; rather, he holds that he brings it only to make himself fit to enter the congregation. For we have not found in the entire Torah [an offering of birds] other than two young birds.
gershom:a2.1: “And the priest shall sacrifice it to the altar,” stated about the voluntary bird offering: why does the verse state it? Was it not already stated: “And he shall sacrifice of the doves”?
gershom:a3.1: I would understand: that he should not bring fewer than two, since the least that “doves” can mean is two.
gershom:a4.1: At any rate, an obligatory [offering] we have not found: in which a single young bird is brought; and these of a convert are obligatory.
gershom:a5.1: In your blood: in the blood of the Paschal offering and the blood of circumcision.
gershom:a6.1: From where do we derive immersion? For it is written: “And Moses took the blood and sprinkled it on the people”; that is sprinkling, and there is a tradition that there is no sprinkling without immersion, for so it is written: “And the pure person shall sprinkle upon the impure on the third day and on the seventh day; and on the seventh day he shall purify him, and he shall wash his clothes” (Numbers 19:19).
gershom:a7.1: “Throughout your generations” is written: that even throughout your generations, at a time when there is no offering, you shall accept converts.
gershom:a8.1: He must set aside a quarter: of a dinar for his nest, so that if the Temple is built he will bring it immediately.
gershom:a9.1: And nullified it due to a mishap: a decree, lest he derive benefit from that money and come to [the transgression of] misuse of consecrated property.
gershom:a10.1: Ger toshav: one who accepted upon himself not to worship idols, and did not accept upon himself the other mitzvot.
gershom:a11.1: Like a Jew on the intermediate days of a Festival: that is, since he has some measure of conversion, he does not perform every labor on Shabbat, unless he has nothing to eat, or it is a matter that would otherwise be lost.
gershom:a12.1: Like a Jew on a Festival: that he performs no other labor except the preparation of food alone.
gershom:a13.1: “With the ram of the guilt offering before the Lord for his sin that he has sinned”: it teaches; since “his sin” is written twice, and “and he shall be forgiven for his sin that he has sinned” is written, twice, [it comes] to make unwitting like intentional with regard to an offering.
gershom:a14.1: For it is written: “And the Lord spoke suddenly”: the divine speech was with them against their will.
gershom:a15.1: “And the thoughtless [peta’im] pass on, and are punished” [the printed text has “suddenly” here and is corrected to “the thoughtless”]: he treats this “thoughtless” like “suddenly”; since it is written “and are punished,” evidently it was intentional.
gershom:a16.1: It is written: “The thoughtless one [peti] believes every word”: and does not understand the essential point; evidently he is unwitting. And even so the Merciful One rendered him liable; “suddenly” is like “thoughtless,” and that is why both are written.
gershom:a17.1: In all of them: those who bring a sliding-scale offering, “and it be hid” is written about them, and here it is not written. But when the verse is written, “And a man who lies carnally with a woman, and she is a maidservant,” it is written about intentional sin, since it is written “there shall be an inspection,” which is lashes; evidently it is intentional. And it is written: “And the priest shall make atonement for him”; so instead of “to make intentional [like unwitting]” for an offering, he should have said unwitting [like intentional].
gershom:a18.1: In one lapse of awareness: that he erred, not knowing that the Torah forbade them.
gershom:a19.1: And what is different from five lapses of awareness with one maidservant, where he brings only one offering, as we learned [in the mishna]: “And one who engages in several acts of intercourse with a maidservant”?
gershom:a20.1: “And unto a woman,” to divide: here too, this “maidservant” is written to divide, for it could have written: “And a man who lies carnally with a woman.”
rashi:b3.1: The naziriteship of purity takes effect from the seventh: therefore, when he became impure twice on the seventh, these are many impurities, since the naziriteship of purity had begun; and with regard to an offering he is liable only once, since this man had not emerged into a time fit for an offering.
rashi:b6.1: “And he shall sanctify his head”: that the naziriteship of purity takes effect on him. On the day of his shaving, and so on.
rashi:b8.1: Mishna. One who warns his wife, etc.: he brings one barley meal offering for all of them when he has her drink.
rashi:b8.2: Who was afflicted with many afflictions: for example, he counted seven [days] and did not manage to bring his offerings before he was afflicted [again], and likewise a second time, and likewise a third.
rashi:b9.1: He brought birds: those two live birds, one for slaughter and one for sending away; and they are not an offering.
rashi:b9.2: They do not count for him: it now enters our mind that this “they do not count for him” means that at the end he must again bring two birds for each and every affliction, until he brings a sin offering; but if he brought birds and his sin offering and was then afflicted, he need not bring [birds] for the first affliction when he becomes pure.
rashi:b13.1: Gemara. But didn’t you say that he brings only one offering: for many afflictions? Evidently it is one long leprosy. Why, then, do you obligate him to bring birds for each affliction?
rashi:b13.2: And to establish [his status] in poverty, etc.: and this is what it says: the birds do not count to establish [his status] in poverty or in wealth. For if he was poor at the time he brought the birds and then became wealthy, he must bring a wealthy man’s offering; and if he was wealthy and became poor, he brings a poor man’s [offering] in his poverty; [this is so] until he brings his sin offering, for we follow the sin offering, whether in poverty or in wealth.
rashi:b15.1: “Whose means do not suffice”: at the time of his purification he brings [the offering] in poverty, even though he later became wealthy.
rashi:b15.2: Rabbi Shimon holds: this “his purification” is the thing that atones for his sin, for afflictions come on account of seven things, in tractate Arakhin (16a).
rashi:b15.3: The thing that renders him fit: the guilt offering, from whose blood they place on his thumbs; it renders him fit for sacrificial food.
rashi:b15.4: Birds: they cause him the beginning of his purification, for they sprinkle on him from the blood of the bird.
rashi:b16.1: Mishna. A woman who gave birth to several offspring: and it explains how: for example, she miscarried within the eighty [days] of a female, and so on. For example, she immersed after the two weeks of impurity, had relations, conceived, and miscarried a female after the forty days of the formation of the fetus, which is fifty-four [days] after the first birth; and she again miscarried at the end of fifty-four days after this one. And that is why it speaks of a female, for with males one cannot say so: if she miscarried within the forty [days] of a male, this second one is mere water, for the fetus is not formed until the fortieth day.
rashi:b17.1: And one who miscarries twins: even males. For example, she conceived three, and miscarried one after forty [days], and the second was delayed and came out within the days of purity of the first, and the third within the days of purity of the second: she brings one offering, for the last, and is exempt [for the others].
rashi:b18.1: Rabbi Yehuda disagrees both about [separate] offspring and about twins, and says: she brings one offering for the first, for the first offspring, and not for the second, because it was born within the completion [of the purification days] of the first. And she brings [one] for the third, because it was not born within a completion, for we do not count a completion for the second, which is as though it does not exist, since it was born within the completion of the first; and the third is the beginning of a [new] birth. And she does not bring an offering for the fourth, since it was born within the completion of the third. But the third was not born within the completion of the first, for there have passed the days of impurity of the first (and the formation of the second and its impurity, and the formation of the third), which is more than eighty from the first. And with twins as well, where Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: for example, where the third was born after the completion of the first; and he is not concerned with the completion of the second, which is as though it does not exist.
rashi:b19.1: Gemara: wherever “the law of” [torat] is written, it implies many.
rashi:b19.2: One might have thought: for the birth and for the ziva [one offering]: for example, she saw [blood] for three days during the days of ziva, stopped on the fourth, and gave birth on the fifth. This is one who gives birth in zov, as we say in Nidda (36b) that she must stop from the discharge close to the birth; and if she did not stop, it is certainly blood caused by the fetus, and she is not one who gives birth in zov.
rashi:b20.1: If that is so: from where would it enter his mind that for the birth and the ziva there is one offering, so that a verse was needed to exclude it? Certainly, if she ate forbidden fat and gave birth, would it enter our minds that she brings one offering for the birth and for the fat? And with ziva too, what does it have to do with birth? [Rashi reads “ate forbidden fat”; the daf reads “consumed blood.”]
rashi:b21.1: “This”: implies that for one birth she brings [one offering for many offspring]; but after the completion she is liable for each one.
rashi:b22.1: According to Rabbi Yehuda: since he does not count a completion for the second, learn from this that the first offspring causes the offering, and she counts eighty days from the first offspring. Therefore the third, which was born after the completion of the first, is a full-fledged offspring with regard to an offering.
rashi:b22.2: According to the Rabbis: who obligate only one [offering], they obligate her for the last, for they hold that the second offspring, that is, the last, causes the offering; and the first, whose days of purity were not completed, has no offering. And from the second we count the completion until the third, and from the third until the fourth, and the completion is not reached until the last.
rashi:b23.1: It is obvious that this is so: for if not, what is their reason?
rashi:b23.2: It was necessary for one who miscarries twins: because of one who miscarries twins the tanna needed to teach us that with one who miscarries twins too, Rabbi Yehuda disagrees. For you might have said that with twins he concedes that it is one long birth, since they were conceived together, and that he also holds there is a completion for the second, so that the third is not subject to an offering.
tosafot:b1.1: “And she is a maidservant,” to divide for each and every maidservant: this is puzzling: here we need [a verse] to divide even though the bodies are separate, whereas there, in the chapter Oto VeEt Beno (Ḥullin 82b), [on] “you shall not slaughter on one day,” it implies that it is obvious he is liable [twice] where he slaughtered it and then slaughtered its offspring, because the bodies are separate, even though there is no verse; and likewise below, in the chapter Amru Lo (Keritot 17a), where they say that Shabbatot are like separate bodies.
tosafot:b10.1: One law for many jealousies: this is puzzling: for in Sota we say that according to the Rabbis a woman does not drink [the water] a second time, and according to Rabbi Yehuda, with one husband and two adulterers she does not drink a second time. And since she does not drink a second time, why is it necessary [to teach] that he brings only one offering?
tosafot:b11.1: One law for many lepers: and in Torat Kohanim it derives this from what is written: “And one ewe lamb” (Leviticus 14:10), which teaches that he brings one for many afflictions; and it expounds “This shall be the law” as one law for all lepers, because we found that the verse distinguished among them in their impurities and in their weeks [of quarantine].
tosafot:b23.1: It was necessary for one who miscarries twins: it might enter your mind that with one who miscarries twins Rabbi Yehuda concedes to the Rabbis. And it is difficult: if so, according to whom does it teach [the case of] one who miscarries twins? If according to the Rabbis, it is obvious; and if according to Rabbi Yehuda, he concedes to the Rabbis. This requires investigation.
gershom:b1.1: (Up to here belongs to 9a.) And a nazirite who became impure several times: who is the tanna? It is Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda. This entire discussion of the nazirite we explained at the beginning of our first chapter.
gershom:b2.1: He brought birds: when he was healed from his leprosy and did not manage to bring his sin offering before he was afflicted again, and he was healed again and brought birds, and was afflicted before he brought his sin offering and his guilt offering. When he is healed again he must bring other birds, and a sin offering for each affliction, for the first ones do not count for him until he brings his sin offering with them.
gershom:b3.1: Rabbi Yehuda says: until he brings his guilt offering: with them.
gershom:b4.1: But didn’t you say that he brings only one offering: for many afflictions?
gershom:b5.1: It is incomplete, and this is what it teaches: he brought birds, and so on; he brings only one offering. And what it says, “they do not count until,” this is what it means: and with regard to establishing [his status] in poverty or wealth, it is not established until he brings the sin offering. That is, if he was poor and brought his sin offering in poverty, then even though he became wealthy before he brought his guilt offering and birds, everything follows the sin offering, and he brings everything in poverty.
gershom:b6.1: Or if he was wealthy and set aside an animal sin offering and became poor, he should wait until he becomes wealthy and bring everything in wealth.
gershom:b7.1: Rabbi Yehuda says: until he brings his guilt offering: for he holds that everything follows the guilt offering.
gershom:b8.1: Atones for him: this is the sin offering.
gershom:b9.1: Renders him fit for sacrificial food: this is the guilt offering.
gershom:b10.1: Causes him purity: the birds, as it is written: “Then the priest shall command to take for him that is to be cleansed two living, pure birds” (Leviticus 14:4).
gershom:b11.1: The woman who miscarried many offspring within the completion [periods], as explained in the mishna: she miscarried within eighty, and so on; she brings one offering for all of them.
gershom:b12.1: One might have thought: even for the birth and for the ziva: that if she gave birth in zov, as we learned in tractate Nidda (36b): “A woman who has difficulty in labor is a nidda; if she had difficulty for three days within the eleven days between one menstrual period and the next, and had a full day’s respite in which she did not see blood, she is a zava,” and afterward she gave birth, this is one who gives birth in zov, and she brings two offerings, one for the birth and one for the ziva. [One might have thought that] she is also exempted with one offering.
gershom:b13.1: The verse states “this”: that is, for the offspring she brings one offering, but not for the birth and for the ziva. [If that is so,] if she ate forbidden fat and gave birth, or ate blood and gave birth, so too would she bring only one offering? Rather, just as she brings two offerings for the fat and for the birth, so too she brings two offerings for the birth and for the ziva.
gershom:b14.1: Rather, say that this is what it asks: since one brings one offering for many offspring, one might have thought that for the birth before the completion and for the birth after the completion she should bring one offering. The verse states “this”: that is, those within the completion are exempted with one offering, but for a birth after the completion she brings another offering. Another version: one might have thought that when she first gave birth in zov, and afterward, after the completion, gave birth again in zov, she brings only two offerings, for the birth and the ziva at first, and for the birth and the ziva after the completion they are exempted [with these], for it is one category of birth and one category of ziva. The verse states “this”: for the first birth she brings two offerings, and for the birth after the completion two offerings.
gershom:b15.1: The woman who miscarried many offspring brings one offering, and so on. How? She gave birth to a female first, and after fourteen days of impurity she conceived a female and miscarried it at the end of forty-one [days], which is within the eighty of the first female. The Rabbis hold that the second offspring nullified the first. What is the reason? Since the time fit to bring an offering for the first, on the eighty-first day, had not arrived, but rather she miscarried another within the completion, the second nullified the first, and from the second she counts eighty for the offering. And if she again miscarried a third offspring within the completion of the second, since the second had not reached [the time for] an offering, the third nullified the second. And so you find that she can miscarry many offspring within the completion of the first, and the Rabbis hold that she always counts from the last. And likewise one who first miscarries twin females: she miscarried one on the first day and one on the second day, so that the second was born within the completion of the first; and on the eightieth day of the second, which is the eighty-first of the first, she again miscarried two twins on two days, the fourth within the completion of the third, according to the Rabbis, who taught that the second nullifies the first. And Rabbi Yehuda says: she always counts eighty for the offering from the first offspring, and whatever she miscarried within its eighty is as though it does not exist. Therefore he says: she brings for the first and does not bring for the second, which she miscarried within the completion of the first; and she brings for the third and does not bring for the fourth, which is within the completion of the third and counts for nothing. And according to Rabbi Yehuda’s reasoning, “the woman who miscarried many offspring” speaks only of two offspring.
gershom:b16.1: The first offspring causes: it is the essential birth.
gershom:b17.1: It is obvious that this is so: for this is what they disagree about; so what does “when you analyze it” teach us?
gershom:b18.1: It was necessary to teach us because of one who miscarries twins, about which we are uncertain: for it might enter your mind that with one who miscarries twins, who were conceived at one time, so that it is one birth, you would say that Rabbi Yehuda concedes to the Rabbis that here we count from the second offspring. “When you analyze it” teaches us that Rabbi Yehuda always holds that we count from the first offspring.
